- **self**: Music, art and creative therapies in PD (14/2)

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Five systematic reviews with meta-analysis of rhythmic auditory cueing, rhythmic auditory stimulation (RAS) or music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease (Ghai, Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li) each report a positive pooled effect on gait velocity or speed and on stride or step length. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5764963/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] The Ye, Wang, Lee and Ko, and Li meta-analyses each report no statistically significant pooled effect of RAS or music-based interventions on cadence in Parkinson's disease. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] Meta-analyses of RAS and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease differ on balance and timed up-and-go (TUG) mobility: Wang and colleagues and Lee and Ko report statistically significant pooled improvements (Berg Balance Scale and TUG for Wang and colleagues; TUG for Lee and Ko), whereas Ye and colleagues report no significant pooled difference for either, and Li and colleagues report a pooled balance effect that became nonsignificant after sensitivity analysis. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait for music-based therapy and RAS in Parkinson's disease: one meta-analysis (K = 6 studies, total N = 168) found no significant effects for UPDRS-motor score or Freezing of Gait, whereas Ye and colleagues (18 studies) report significant pooled improvements in UPDRS-III and in the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22166406/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/
- [statement] Authors of RAS and music-based meta-analyses in Parkinson's disease state evidence-quality limits themselves: Ye and colleagues note that only two included studies had more than 100 subjects and thirteen had fewer than 50; Wang and colleagues report that lack of blinding of participants and trainers was the most common risk of bias, with twelve studies at high risk for this reason, and that the largest included study had 90 participants; Lee and Ko state that allocation concealment and blinding were not possible in most trials because of the nature of the music-related activities; and Li and colleagues rated the overall methodological quality of the included RCTs as moderate. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9366143/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9053573/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12580135/
- [statement] Meta-analyses differ on non-motor outcomes of music-based or arts-based interventions in Parkinson's disease: Lee and Ko report no significant pooled effect on quality of life (SMD = −0.68, p = 0.18), and Liu and colleagues' meta-analysis of 22 studies (928 participants) reports non-significant effects on quality of life, cognition and depressive symptoms, whereas a music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies including 3635 patients (searched from inception to 31 August 2026) reports significant improvements in depression, anxiety and life quality. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9859027/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13281054/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43076026/
- [statement] A systematic review of randomized controlled trials of music-based interventions for cognitive rehabilitation in Parkinson's disease, which analyzed three articles, concluded that the results showed no evidence of efficacy for cognitive outcomes, and a randomized trial of a group-based music intervention that enrolled forty-six patients (Pohl and colleagues) states that it does not support efficacy for immediate or lasting gains in dual-tasking, cognition, balance, or freezing of gait. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10415237/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7132435/
- [statement] Trinchillo and colleagues' review states that Butala and colleagues found significant improvements in motor functions after 24 weeks in a randomized crossover trial of weekly group singing, whereas Butala and colleagues' own Parkinsonics trial report states a significant overall-cohort MDS-UPDRS Part III improvement at 24 weeks (Δ = 5.9 points) that became nonsignificant when the baseline was adjusted in mixed linear model analyses, and that they cannot conclusively attribute motor improvements to the singing intervention. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13731696/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9553721/
- [statement] Two recent systematic reviews of singing in Parkinson's disease word their conclusions differently: Irons and Sheffield (23 studies, 540 participants; last search 3 April 2025) rate the certainty of the one RCT-based favourable outcome as very low and state that, due to insufficient high-quality evidence, they are unable to determine the effects of singing interventions, whereas Trinchillo and colleagues (twenty-six studies, 1057 patients; considerable heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis) conclude that singing is a promising adjunct therapy. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645629/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13731696/
- [statement] A systematic review of active group-based performing arts interventions in Parkinson's disease (searches conducted in February 2020) included fifty-six studies reported in 67 publications with a total of 1531 people with PD; dance was studied most (38 studies), followed by 12 studies on singing, four on music therapy and two on theatrical interventions, and the authors state that no studies compared interventions from different performing arts modalities. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547481/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
- [statement] Reviews and a patient-organisation page describe the creative-therapy evidence base in Parkinson's disease as limited by small samples and weak designs: Barnish and Barran list small sample sizes and the absence of control groups in over half of the included studies among the main methodological concerns, Irons and Sheffield report that most singing studies' methods were not rated highly due to small sample sizes, blinding and weak study design, and the American Parkinson Disease Association page states that most complementary therapies, which it lists as including singing, music therapy, dance therapy, theater and art therapy, have usually been studied only in small groups of people. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547481/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12645629/, https://www.apdaparkinson.org/article/music-therapy-parkinsons-disease/
- [statement] On visual-art therapy in Parkinson's disease, an observational, prospective, open-label, exploratory study of eighteen patients reported improved Navon test, eye-tracking and UPDRS performance after twenty sessions of art therapy, whereas the authors of an art-therapy meta-analysis state that visual arts and painting represent a significant research gap whose direct therapeutic effects remain unexplored. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33526323/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12444631/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] In the ParkinSong controlled trial of 75 people living with Parkinson's disease, which compared a singing-based intervention with an active control condition at 2 dosage levels (weekly vs monthly) over 3 months, intervention participants showed significant improvements in vocal intensity, maximum expiratory pressure and voice-related quality of life compared with controls, with no statistical differences between groups on maximum phonation length or maximum inspiratory pressure at 3 months; a systematic review describes this trial as a non-randomised controlled trial. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31081485/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7547481/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] In the 'art therapy' meta-analysis by Liu and colleagues of 26 randomized controlled trials (2,756 individuals), the included interventions were 5 music, 14 dance, 2 yoga, 1 mindfulness, 1 theater, 1 virtual-reality game-based, 1 Tai Chi plus yoga and 1 Qigong plus dance studies, and the authors conclude that dance therapy exhibited the most pronounced effects across motor function outcomes. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12444631/ · keywords: Music, art and creative therapies in PD

## Research summary — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Educational summary of what published sources say, not medical advice. Meta-analyses of rhythmic auditory stimulation and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease report positive pooled effects on gait velocity and stride length but not cadence, and disagree on balance, timed up-and-go, UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait. One singing review rates the certainty of its RCT-based finding as very low and another calls singing a promising adjunct therapy, and a trial's own authors limit attribution to singing. Reviews conflict on quality of life, mood and cognition. The visual art therapy evidence cited here is an exploratory observational study, and a meta-analysis calls visual arts and painting a research gap; one art-therapy meta-analysis of 26 trials included 14 dance trials. Review authors repeatedly flag small samples and limited blinding.

## Source disagreement — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Balance and timed up-and-go: Wang and colleagues report statistically significant pooled improvements, while Ye and colleagues report no significant pooled difference for either.

## Source disagreement — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

UPDRS motor score and freezing of gait: one meta-analysis (K = 6 studies, total N = 168) found no significant effects, while Ye and colleagues report significant improvements in UPDRS-III and the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire.

## Source disagreement — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Quality of life, cognition and mood: Lee and Ko report no significant pooled effects on quality of life and cognition and Liu and colleagues report no significant pooled effects on quality of life, cognition or depressive symptoms, while a music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies reports significant improvements in depression, anxiety and life quality.

## Source disagreement — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Singing: Irons and Sheffield state they are unable to determine the effects of singing interventions, while Trinchillo and colleagues conclude that singing is a promising adjunct therapy.

## Source disagreement — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Parkinsonics: Trinchillo and colleagues state that Butala and colleagues found significant motor improvements after 24 weeks, while Butala and colleagues state they cannot conclusively attribute motor improvements to the singing intervention.

## Open question — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Whether benefits persist after interventions end: Pohl and colleagues report between-group differences in the Falls Efficacy Scale and Parkinson Disease Questionnaire-39 items that were not maintained at three months post-intervention, while Butala and colleagues report that some improvements were sustained at least six weeks after interventions ended.

## Open question — Music, art and creative therapies in PD

Which randomized trials of visual art therapy in Parkinson's disease exist beyond the exploratory observational study of eighteen patients, given the meta-analysis authors' statement that visual arts and painting represent a significant research gap.
